study.title: Psalm 120 - Clarment of the righteous in the midst of lies and hostility
study.overview: This psalm opens the group of songs of the steps with a prayer of deliverance. The psalmist begins by remembering that in his affliction he cried out to the LORD and was heard. He then describes the danger of false words: liar lips and misleading tongue. The center of the psalm shows that God does not leave injustice without answer; aggressive and fraudulent language will be judged. Finally, the poet regrets living among people hostile to peace, using the image of being in Meseque and in the tents of Quedar to express isolation, continuous tension and coexistence with violent people.

outline.title: Clamor ear and request for deliverance
outline.explanation: The psalmist declares that in the troubles he cried out to the LORD and received an answer. Next, he asks that his life be delivered from the lie and deceitful speech, showing that oppression begins in the word and slander.

outline.title: The question about the judgment against the false language
outline.explanation: The poem turns directly to the verbal aggressor and asks what will be given to it. The implicit answer is of judgment: sharp arrows and burning coals, an image of severe and certain punishment against falsehood.

outline.title: Foreigner among the enemies of peace
outline.explanation: The psalmist laments his long stay among peoples described as violent and hostile. He identifies with peace, but his speech is received with war, revealing the pain of seeking reconciliation in an environment that rejects peace.

study.context: The notes present this psalm as one of the songs of the steps, associated with the pilgrimage to worship in Jerusalem at the national feasts. The title is linked by some interpreters to the idea of "subida" or "they", but the explanation of the title itself is treated with caution in the notes. Matthew Henry notes that these psalms can have diverse uses, including personal and community, and that the exact meaning of the title is uncertain.
study.theology: The psalm affirms, first of all, God's attention to the cry of the afflicted: prayer is not empty, for the Lord answers. He then teaches that lies and slander are not light sins; they hurt people and corrupt their coexistence, so they attract divine judgment. The image of arrows and coals shows that God acts with righteousness against the evil practiced by means of the word. Finally, the text reveals the conflict between the desire for peace of the just and the bellicose disposition of those around him. Peace here is not a mere absence of quarrels, but a moral stance that contrasts with verbal and social violence. The psalm can also be read as the voice of God's people in a hostile environment, even though the concrete application of the language on Month and Quedar is discussed by commentators as literal or figurative.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist presents his life as that of a foreigner between liars and hostile people, showing alienation and continuous conflict.
The psalm shows deliverance obtained through prayer against the false language, highlighting the destructive effect of lies and slander.
The response to the verbal aggressor is described as severe judgment, figured by sharp arrows and burning coals.

questions: How does God's response to the afflicted cry confront our temptation to solve everything by human means?
In what ways do lies, slander and aggressive speech still hurt communion between people and churches?
What does it mean, in practice, to declare: "I am of peace," when the people around prefer conflict?
study.practice: Pray specificly when you target false or unfair words instead of reduing to the same extent. Examine your own speech: eliminate exaggerations, half-truths and comments that inflate conflicts. Try to be someone who promotes peace in a concrete way, listening patiently, speaking honestly and refusing to feed unnecessary disputes.
study.uncertainty: The title of the group of the songs of the steps has proposed explanations, but the notes do not allow to safely complete their exact meaning. It is also not possible to define with certainty, only based on these notes, whether Month and Quedar should be understood in a literal or mainly figurative way; the commentators present both possibilities.
